blocks.text: You send ten products to ten creators, get ten pieces of content back, and three of them actually sell. The next month you repeat the whole process from scratch with ten different people, because that's what a one-off campaign is. Meanwhile one of your best-performing creators from last quarter never hears from you again.
Long term creator partnerships vs one off posts: which drives more sales

Long term partnerships win on sales over time because the creator's audience starts to trust the recommendation after seeing it more than once, and the creator gets better at selling your product with each collaboration. One-off posts win on speed and reach when you need a quick burst of content or you're still working out which creators actually convert for your brand. Most brands need both: one-off collaborations to find the people worth repeating with, and repeat arrangements with the handful who prove themselves.

The mistake is treating every collaboration as a one-off by default. If a creator's content drove tracked sales, that's a signal to go back to them, not a reason to move on to someone new for variety's sake.

A single post from a creator their audience has never heard mention your brand before reads as an ad, even when it's genuinely good content. The same creator posting about your product a second or third time reads as a habit, something they actually use. That shift changes how the audience responds, and it's the main reason repeat creators tend to outperform new ones on the same product.

There's a production benefit too. A creator who has already made content for you knows your product, your brand voice and what you need without a full brief each time. You spend less time on revisions and more time with usable content. If you've used a [creator brief template](/blog/creator-brief-template-for-ecommerce) to get a new creator up to speed once, you'll notice the second brief takes a fraction of the back and forth.

Say you run a coffee subscription brand and one creator's first gifted post brings in a handful of tracked orders through their link. Instead of moving to the next name on your list, you ask them to do a second video a month later, maybe a brew tutorial instead of an unboxing. By the third collaboration their audience expects to see your bags in their kitchen, and the conversion on that link is consistently higher than it was on the first post.
How to structure an ambassador arrangement

An ambassador arrangement is just a repeat collaboration with terms set in advance instead of negotiated fresh each time. Agree on a cadence (monthly content, a set number of posts per quarter), a mix of payment types if it suits both sides, and what happens if performance drops. Put it in writing the same way you would any paid collaboration, covering usage rights and exclusivity if you need either. Our [creator contract essentials](/blog/creator-contract-essentials-small-brands) post covers the terms worth locking down before the second collaboration, not just the first.

Payment structure matters more here than in a one-off. A flat fee for every post regardless of performance can get expensive if the content stops converting. An affiliate commission on tracked sales rewards creators for staying effective and costs you less when a particular post underperforms. Many ambassador deals mix the two: a smaller fixed fee plus commission, so the creator isn't entirely dependent on sales they can't fully control. If you're deciding between structures, [gifted vs paid creator collaborations](/blog/gifted-vs-paid-creator-collaborations) and [affiliate commission rates for creators](/blog/affiliate-commission-rates-for-creators) both walk through the trade-offs in more detail. On Linkable, affiliate sales are tracked through unique creator links and discount codes with commission payouts handled through the platform, which makes an ongoing arrangement easier to manage than chasing receipts by hand.
When one-off collaborations are still the right call

One-off posts make sense when you're launching a new product and need a wide spread of first impressions rather than depth with a few people, when you're testing a new platform or format and don't yet know who performs well there, or when budget only stretches to a single gifted send. They're also the right starting point with any new creator, because you shouldn't commit to an ongoing arrangement before you've seen what they actually produce. Our [evaluate a creator before working with them](/blog/how-to-evaluate-a-creator-before-working-with-them) post covers what to check before the first collaboration, let alone the fifth.

Seasonal moments are another case. A Q4 push often needs a larger spread of creators posting once each rather than a small ambassador roster posting repeatedly, simply because you need reach across more audiences in a short window. Our [Q4 creator campaign timeline](/blog/q4-creator-campaign-timeline) is built around that kind of spread.
Building the pipeline that feeds both

The brands that run this well don't choose long term versus one-off upfront. They run a steady flow of one-off collaborations to keep finding new people, then promote the ones who perform into repeat arrangements. That funnel only works if you can see performance per creator clearly, which is where campaign and creator insights matter more than they first seem to. Linkable's reporting shows content delivered, audiences reached, engagement generated and tracked sales per creator, so the decision to repeat with someone isn't a guess based on how the content looked, it's based on what it actually sold.

This week, pull up your last two or three campaigns and look at which creators' links or codes actually drove sales. Reach out to the two or three strongest performers with a second brief rather than adding them to a general thank-you list, and start treating that shortlist as the beginning of an ambassador roster rather than a one-off that happened to go well.

faqs.a: There's no fixed number, but most brands treat a second paid or affiliate collaboration with the same creator as the start of an ongoing arrangement, especially once a cadence is agreed rather than negotiated fresh each time.
faqs.q: How many posts before a creator counts as an ambassador rather than a one-off

faqs.a: Yes, or at least an addendum. A one-off contract usually covers a single deliverable and usage window, while an ambassador arrangement needs cadence, renewal or exit terms, and clarity on what happens if a post underperforms.
faqs.q: Do ambassador creators need a different contract to one-off creators

faqs.a: Yes. A smaller flat fee combined with affiliate commission keeps ongoing costs tied to performance, and gifted product can still form part of the arrangement for creators who are happy to be paid mostly in commission.
faqs.q: Can a brand run long term partnerships without a large budget

faqs.a: No. Only creators whose content measurably sold are worth repeating with. Posting again with someone whose first collaboration didn't convert usually just repeats the same result.
faqs.q: Should every creator eventually move from one-off to long term
